say: A cohort is a group of customers who started in the same month. It is more honest than total sales, which can rise with more ads while old customers quietly leave.
For example, Ada in Lagos had 80 first-time buyers in January.
In February, 32 of them ordered again. That is 40 percent month-1 retention.
In February she added a free dessert on every fourth order. Of February's 100 first-time buyers, 45 came back in March: 45 percent.
She checks for other causes, finds none, and logs it as promising, not proven, because it was not a controlled test.
Use this template: because we saw this evidence, we believe this change will raise a metric from a baseline to a target, within a time.
For example: because 18 of 30 lost chats asked about delivery days, a quick reply with delivery days...

panel.heading: Write a hypothesis that can fail
items: Because we saw: 18 of 30 lost chats
We believe: a quick reply with delivery days

say: ...will raise chat-to-order from 30% to 36% within four weeks. Better branding will help is not a hypothesis. It can never be proven wrong.

say: Write the metric, the sample size and the end date in your log before launching. Otherwise you will be tempted to stop the day it looks good.

panel.rule: Fix the metric, sample size and end date before you start.

say: ICE scores each idea from 1 to 10 on Impact, Confidence and Ease, then averages them. Ada's quick reply scores 6, 8 and 10, an ICE of 8.0. The dessert scores 6.3, a new ad 5.7.
Building her own app scores 4.3. Its imagined impact is large, but effort is high and evidence is thin. RICE, which adds reach and effort in person-weeks, also puts the quick reply first.

Small samples swing randomly and look like results. A rule of thumb for the people you need per group is 16, times your baseline rate, times one minus that rate, divided by the change you care about, squared.

panel.heading: Low traffic? Test big changes
items: Per group = 16 x p x (1 - p) / d squared

say: For example, Ngozi's fabric store gets about 1,800 visitors a month, with a 10% add-to-cart rate. To spot a change to 12% she needs 3,600 per group. That would take 4 months.

panel.heading: Low traffic? Test big changes
items: Per group = 16 x p x (1 - p) / d squared

say: To spot a change to 14% she needs only 900 per group, about one month. So she tests a bold change, not a tiny button colour.

panel.heading: Low traffic? Test big changes
items: Per group = 16 x p x (1 - p) / d squared

say: For example, Amaka tests a shorter checkout for 14 days. A gets 100 purchases from 2,000 visitors, 5.0%. B gets 130, 6.5%. Her z value is about 2.04, just above 1.96, so it is significant at the 5% level. Refunds stayed at 3 in each group.

panel.heading: Real win or false win?
left: Sample and date fixed in advance

say: Be suspicious of a test stopped the moment B looked ahead, one that ran only a few days, or one comparing this month with last. And name one main metric in advance.

panel.heading: Real win or false win?
left: Sample and date fixed in advance

say: A guardrail is a metric that must not get worse while you chase the main one. Discounts can lift orders but cut profit. Daily broadcasts can lift clicks but bring blocks.

cards.d: Watch gross margin, refunds and complaints, opt-outs or blocks, and delivery time.
Message only people who opted in. Easy opt-out. Never buy or scrape contact lists.
No fake countdowns, hidden fees, pre-ticked boxes or fake only 2 left messages.

say: The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 requires a lawful basis, such as consent. Keep customer sheets private, and never post screenshots showing customer numbers.

say: To remember. Track every stage and read retention by cohort. Write a hypothesis that can fail, and rank ideas before testing. Fix the rules in advance, do not peek, and protect customers while you grow.
